analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal institute to develop drugs with public patents and license them to competing manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2004 and referred to a House subcommittee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new federal institute that takes discoveries from government-funded research, keeps the patents in public hands, and develops promising drugs through federal laboratories. Rather than handing patents to one company that can charge whatever the market will bear, the government would license approved drugs non-exclusively, so multiple companies could manufacture them and compete on price. The bill authorized roughly $20 billion a year for this work.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay for prescription drugs, especially the growing share priced out by rising costs. The bill's own findings note drug costs rose at a 19.1% annual rate over the prior eight years and that US prices far exceed those of other developed countries because patents grant drug companies monopolies with no price limits. Competitive, non-exclusive manufacturing of government-patented drugs would push prices toward the cost of production. Taxpayers would also benefit twice over from research they already fund, instead of paying monopoly prices on top.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would make drugs developed with federal patents available 'to the public at reasonable prices' by requiring non-exclusive licenses, so several manufacturers could compete rather than one patent-holder charging monopoly prices.

It would prohibit the government from transferring ownership of patents on candidate discoveries to any private entity — directly reversing the existing practice (under Bayh-Dole) of handing publicly funded inventions to private companies — and let citizens sue to enforce that rule.

It would establish ten federal laboratories within NIH and require all raw research data to be posted publicly, addressing the bill's finding that industry-funded drug research suffers from concealed findings, bias, and secrecy.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, whose core business model — holding patent monopolies on drugs and charging prices with no restriction — would face direct public competition. The bill would cost taxpayers up to about $20 billion a year in appropriations, a cost weighed against the drug prices patients currently pay.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorized about $19.9 billion for fiscal 2004 rising to about $21.97 billion by 2008, a substantial new federal spending commitment at a time when NIH's entire budget was itself on the order of $28 billion.

It bets that government laboratories can pick promising compounds and run drug development at least as well as private industry, and it weakens the patent incentives — the main current driver of private drug investment — for any discovery the federal government touches, with no guarantee the savings to patients would exceed the cost to taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside for patients is large: an estimated multi-billion-dollar shift of drug development into the public domain, with non-exclusive licensing aimed squarely at the monopoly pricing that makes US drugs the most expensive in the developed world. The risks are real too — roughly $20 billion a year in new appropriations and uncertainty about whether federal labs can outperform private industry at drug development. But the bill never advanced far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested; it died in a subcommittee without a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee on October 8, 2004, and never received a hearing or vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the Free Market Drug Act in the House on September 28, 2004.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which never acted on it.
On October 8, 2004, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action of any kind followed for the remainder of the Congress.
The bill attracted 9 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Senate companion movement appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies kept their patent monopolies and their freedom to charge unrestricted prices; patients continued to bear US drug prices that the bill's own findings called the highest in the developed world.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 9 cosponsors; the bill bore his name alone on introduction.

for.name: 9 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and referred it to its Health Subcommittee without scheduling a markup or hearing.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health, House Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from October 8, 2004 onward; no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred before the Congress ended.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturing industry
against.role: Industry whose patent-monopoly pricing model the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: The bill would have ended the industry's practice of acquiring patents on federally funded discoveries and subjected its market to public competition; industry lobbying against such measures was a fixture of the era.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a progressive Democrat; no Republican support appears anywhere in the record.

industries.note: The bill attacks the industry's core revenue engine: patent monopolies on drugs with no price restrictions, which the bill's findings credit for US prices being the highest in the developed world. Federal ownership of patents on publicly funded discoveries, plus mandatory non-exclusive licensing, would end the industry's exclusive control over drugs built on public research.

Non-exclusive licenses would open government-patented drugs to multiple competing manufacturers, creating new business for companies that profit by producing drugs cheaply rather than by holding patents.
The bill covers biological products and devices as well as drugs, so its federal-patent and non-exclusive-license rules would apply to the biotech and device sectors' patented-product model too.
Research and development would flow through cooperative agreements and contracts with private entities, but only under federal patents and non-exclusive licenses — paid work, stripped of ownership.
